title: Driving in the Dark: Realtime Denoising of Minimally Dosed High-speed Digital Electron Counted STEM
content: The scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM) is a powerful instrument, delivering imaging and chemical information down to the atomic scale. As with any technique that uses a tightly focused beam of irradiation, sample heating, drift, damage, or charging are always risks the operator must face. Recently, several new techniques have been developed to improve the speed and sensitivity of low-dose imaging including; digital detection at greatly reduced beam-currents [1], minimizing the time spent dwelling on each pixel [2], or intra-pixel blanking to reduce the fraction of each pixel exposed to the beam [3]. Together these techniques enable the rapid acquisition of digital data limited only by Poisson noise. However, with such ultra-low-dose acquisition, it is often difficult to recognize any high-resolution structures unless images are accumulated (frame-averaged). Regrettably, if there is sample drift, simple accumulation will blur the image – where the directionality of a slow drift will impart a blurring that looks similar to the effects of astigmatism. Fortunately, many crystalline samples appear periodic at high magnification and this can be used to design image reconstruction methods.
